t.1.26.1: Sūta said: As soon as it was merely touched by the feet of the mighty Garuḍa, that branch of the tree broke, and he held it up as it broke.
t.1.26.2: Smiling, he gazed upon that great broken branch, and then he saw the Vālakhilyas hanging there, heads downward.
t.1.26.4: Thus he, together with the elephant and the tortoise, flew over many lands out of compassion for the Vālakhilyas, but he found no place to alight.
t.1.26.3: Terrified that they would be destroyed, the lord of birds flew after the branch and seized it in his beak, out of concern for them alone; then the bird slowly flew about, shattering the mountains.
t.1.26.5: Having gone to Gandhamādana, the imperishable best of mountains, he saw there his father Kaśyapa, engaged in austerity.
t.1.26.6: And his father, too, saw that bird of divine form, endowed with splendour, valour and strength, and swift as the mind and the wind.
t.1.26.8: Him, bearing magic power and might, like fire itself blazing and raised up, unassailable and unconquerable by gods, Dānavas and Rākṣasas.
t.1.26.7: Him who resembled a mountain peak, like the upraised staff of Brahmā, inconceivable, unknowable, striking terror into all beings.
t.1.26.10: Then the blessed Kaśyapa, seeing him arrive and knowing his intention, spoke these words.
t.1.26.9: He was the splitter of mountain peaks, the drier-up of river waters, the terrible churner of the worlds, whose appearance was like that of Kṛtānta, Death himself.
t.1.26.12: For the sake of his son, Kaśyapa sought to appease those Vālakhilyas, perfected through austerity, pointing to this as the reason.
t.1.26.11: Son, do not act rashly, lest you meet with sudden suffering; may the Vālakhilyas, drinkers of the sun's rays, not burn you in their wrath.
t.1.26.13: O ascetics rich in austerity, Garuḍa's undertaking is for the welfare of creatures; he wishes to accomplish a great deed, and you should grant him leave for it.
t.1.26.15: Then, when they had departed, the son of Vinatā, his mouth still burdened with the branch, questioned his father Kaśyapa.
t.1.26.14: Thus addressed by the Blessed One, those sages let go of the branch and went to the holy mountain Himavant, seeking austerities.
t.1.26.16: Blessed one, where shall I let go of this branch of the tree? Let the blessed one tell me of a region devoid of brāhmaṇas.
t.1.26.17: Then Kaśyapa told him of a mountain empty of men, its caves blocked with snow, unreachable by others even in thought.
t.1.26.18: Having first entered with his mind that great hollow of the mountain, the bird Tārkṣya flew swiftly toward it, carrying the branch, the elephant and the tortoise.
t.1.26.20: Then Garuḍa, the best of flying creatures, having traversed a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas in no very great time, arrived there.
t.1.26.19: Not even a thong made of a hundred hides, whether thick or thin, could encircle that huge branch of the tree which the bird seized and carried off as he went.
t.1.26.22: Struck by the wind of his wings, that king of mountains trembled, and, its trees dropping down, it released a shower of flowers.
t.1.26.21: At his father's word, the sky-goer reached that mountain in but a moment and there let fall the great branch with a resounding crash.
t.1.26.23: And all around, the peaks of that mountain shattered, peaks variegated with gems and gold that had adorned the great mountain.
t.1.26.24: And many trees too, struck by that branch, shone with their golden blossoms like rain clouds lit with lightning.
t.1.26.25: There those trees, golden-blossomed and further joined with the mountain's minerals, shone brilliantly, tinged by the rays of the sun.
t.1.26.26: Then, having settled upon the peak of that mountain, Garuḍa, that best of birds, devoured both of them, the elephant and the tortoise.
t.1.26.27: Then, swift as thought, he flew up from the top of the mountain peak; and portents foretelling fear for the gods began to appear.
t.1.26.28: Indra's beloved vajra blazed up as if stricken with distress, and a meteor, smoking and flaming, fell from the sky, dislodged from the heavens.
t.1.26.29: Likewise the weapons of the Vasus, the Rudras and the Ādityas, all of them, of the Sādhyas and the Maruts, and of whatever other hosts of deities there were, each one's own weapon, rushed against one another.
t.1.26.31: And the sky, though cloudless, thundered with a mighty roar; and he who is the god even of the gods then rained down blood.
t.1.26.30: Then, as had never happened before, not even in the battle of the gods and asuras, winds blew with crashes of thunder and meteors fell on every side.
t.1.26.32: The garlands of the gods withered, and their splendors were quenched; dreadful clouds of evil portent rained down much blood, and clouds of dust that rose up sullied their crowns.
t.1.26.33: Then Śatakratu, together with the gods, agitated with fear and seeing the dreadful portents, spoke thus to Bṛhaspati.
t.1.26.34: Why, O blessed one, have these terrible great portents arisen? Yet I see no enemy who could overpower us in battle.
t.1.26.35: Bṛhaspati said: Through your offence, lord of the gods, and through your carelessness, Śatakratu, a wondrous being has come into existence by the austerity of the Vālakhilyas.
t.1.26.36: The son of the sage Kaśyapa and of Vinatā, a sky-ranging bird, mighty and able to take any form at will, has arrived to carry off the Soma.
t.1.26.37: This bird, the best of the mighty, is able to carry off the soma. I deem everything possible in him; he could accomplish even what cannot be accomplished.
t.1.26.38: Having heard these words, Śakra spoke to the guardians of the amṛta: "A bird of great valor and strength has set out to carry off the soma from here."
t.1.26.40: Hearing those words, the astonished gods made a determined effort and stood surrounding the amṛta, and so did Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, Śatakratu.
t.1.26.39: I hereby warn you all, so that he may not carry it off by force, for his strength is unequalled; so Bṛhaspati told me.
t.1.26.41: The high-spirited ones, wearing very costly coats of mail, golden and many-hued, and wrought with lapis lazuli.
t.1.26.42: And raising by the thousands weapons of many kinds, terrible in form, in great numbers, with whetted, sharp points and edges,
t.1.26.43: Discs everywhere, blazing with sparks and flames and wreathed in smoke, as well as iron clubs, tridents and battle-axes.
t.1.26.45: With those radiant weapons, the hosts of gods, adorned with celestial ornaments, stood there shining, their faint-heartedness gone.
t.1.26.44: Taking up various sharp spears, spotless swords, and maces fearsome to behold, weapons befitting their own bodies,
t.1.26.46: The gods, of matchless strength, valor and splendor, their minds set firmly on guarding the amṛta, destroyers of the cities of the Asuras, shone with bodies blazing like kindled fire.
t.1.26.47: Thus that great battle, held by the gods and crowded with hundreds of thousands of iron clubs, shone forth, lit by the rays of the sun, as if it had dropped down into the midst of the sky.
